official_title: Shall the City Charter of the City of Houston be amended to 1) require the Houston Police Department to make enforcement of Class A and Class B misdemeanor marijuana possession its lowest law-enforcement priority with related reporting requirements and 2) prohibit Houston police officers from requesting or executing "no-knock" search warrants?
plain_summary: One vote covers two separate policies. First, Houston police would have to make misdemeanor marijuana possession their lowest enforcement priority, with an audit and yearly public reports. Second, officers could not request or serve no-knock search warrants. It does not legalize marijuana.
yes_means: A YES vote adds both rules to the city charter: misdemeanor marijuana possession becomes HPD's lowest priority (with an audit and yearly reports), and no-knock warrants are banned.
no_means: A NO vote leaves the charter unchanged; HPD keeps setting its marijuana enforcement and no-knock warrant rules through department policy, which city leaders can change.
current_law: Marijuana possession is still illegal under Texas law; up to four ounces is a misdemeanor. After the 2019 Harding Street raid, HPD adopted a department policy limiting no-knock warrants. A new state law limiting district attorneys' discretion has put the Harris County DA's marijuana diversion program in question.
fiscal_impact: No official city cost estimate was found. The full text requires a one-time audit (due within 120 days) and yearly reports, and tells the city to report what it spends on THC testing. FOX 26 said it could not verify the campaign's cost and savings figures.
confusing_wording_note: One YES or NO covers two different policies, marijuana enforcement and the no-knock warrant ban. You cannot vote on them separately. "Lowest priority" does not legalize marijuana, and officers keep discretion to arrest or cite. The audit and yearly reports are in the full charter text, not the ballot words. Some news coverage says the measure bars using marijuana odor as a reason to search; the official text posted by the city has no odor rule.

supporters_case.text: Ground Game Texas, the group behind the petition, says writing the rules into the charter keeps them in place when city leaders change, reduces unequal enforcement, and keeps a low-level arrest from costing people jobs and homes. It says the no-knock ban, inspired by the 2019 Harding Street raid, protects both residents and officers.

opponents_case.text: No organized "vote no" campaign was found. South Texas College of Law Houston professor Tom Hogan opposes a blanket ban, saying no-knock warrants should stay available for rare, high-risk cases with judges as the check. He also notes a lower priority does not stop officers from enforcing the law.

jurisdiction: Cypress-Fairbanks ISD (northwest Harris County, including part of northwest Houston)
official_title: This is a tax increase Ratifying the ad valorem tax rate of $1.1569 in Cypress-Fairbanks Independent School District for the current year, a rate that will result in an increase of 23 percent in maintenance and operations tax revenue for the district for the current year as compared to the preceding year, which is an additional $102,350,532.
plain_summary: Asks Cy-Fair ISD voters to approve the $1.1569 per $100 tax rate the board adopted for this year. The ballot says that raises day-to-day operating money by 23%, about $102.4 million more than last year.
yes_means: A YES vote approves the $1.1569 rate and the extra $102.4 million for operations.
no_means: A NO vote rolls the rate back to the voter-approval rate, and the district does not get the extra $102.4 million.
fiscal_impact: An additional $102,350,532 in operating (maintenance and operations) revenue, per the ballot. The district's election order says the adopted total rate of $1.1569 is up from $1.0669 last year: the operating part rises from $0.6669 to $0.7869, while the debt part falls from $0.40 to $0.37. Your own bill depends on your appraised value and exemptions.
confusing_wording_note: State law requires every school tax rate election to open with "This is a tax increase" (printed in capitals on the ballot). Here the total rate does go up, by 9 cents per $100. The 23% is growth in the district's operating revenue, not your bill. This is separate from the four bond questions (B to E), which pay for buildings and equipment.

jurisdiction: Cypress-Fairbanks ISD (northwest Harris County, including part of northwest Houston)
official_title: This is a property tax increase. The issuance of $1,299,520,000 of bonds for the improvement, capital renovation, repair and replacement, and equipment of and additions to existing school buildings in the District, for the purchase of new school buses, for the retrofitting of school buses with emergency, safety, or security equipment, and for the purchase or retrofitting of vehicles to be used for emergency, safety, or security purposes, and the levying of a tax sufficient to pay the principal of and interest on the bonds and to pay the costs of any credit agreements executed or authorized in anticipation of, in relation to or in connection with the bonds.
plain_summary: Lets Cy-Fair ISD borrow up to $1.3 billion to repair, renovate and add on to existing schools, buy new buses, and add safety equipment to buses and security vehicles.
yes_means: A YES vote lets the district sell up to $1,299,520,000 in bonds for these projects and repay them with property taxes.
no_means: A NO vote means the district cannot sell these bonds.
current_law: Cy-Fair ISD owes $3,264,440,000 in principal on existing debt (about $4.6 billion with interest) and levies a $0.40 per $100 debt tax.
fiscal_impact: District estimate: $2,837,363,167 in principal and interest, with the bonds sold in five yearly batches from 2026 to 2030. The district says Props B through E together could be paid while lowering its debt tax rate from $0.40 to $0.37 per $100. The district's "$0 added tax on a $100,000 homestead" estimate reflects that a $100,000 homestead owes no school tax at all after the state's $140,000 homestead exemption.
confusing_wording_note: State law requires school bond questions to open with "This is a property tax increase" (printed in capitals on the ballot), even when, as here, the district projects its debt tax rate will go down. Prop A on the same ballot would raise the district's operating rate.

jurisdiction: Spring ISD (north Harris County, including part of north Houston)
official_title: This is a tax increase Ratifying the ad valorem tax rate of $1.1569 in Spring Independent School District for the current year, a rate that will result in an increase of 0 percent in maintenance and operations tax revenue for the district for the current year as compared to the preceding year, which is an additional $0.
plain_summary: Asks Spring ISD voters to approve the $1.1569 per $100 tax rate the board adopted for this year. The required ballot wording says it raises operating revenue by 0%, an additional $0.
yes_means: A YES vote approves the $1.1569 rate the board adopted.
no_means: A NO vote rolls the rate back to the voter-approval rate.
fiscal_impact: The ballot language states a 0 percent increase and an additional $0 in maintenance and operations revenue. We found no district explanation of why an election is needed at 0%.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot opens with "This is a tax increase" (printed in capitals) and then says the increase is 0 percent and $0. State law requires the opening phrase on every school tax rate election. The rate shown matches Cy-Fair ISD's exactly, so check the wording on your own ballot at harrisvotes.com.

jurisdiction: Huffman ISD (northeast Harris County, touching Houston's Lake Houston area)
official_title: This is a tax increase Ratifying the ad valorem tax rate of $1.0637 in Huffman Independent School District for the current year, a rate that will result in an increase of 4.88 percent in maintenance and operations tax revenue for the district for the current year as compared to the preceding year, which is an additional $ -20.30.
plain_summary: Asks Huffman ISD voters to approve the $1.0637 per $100 tax rate the board adopted, which the ballot says raises operating revenue 4.88%.
yes_means: A YES vote approves the $1.0637 rate.
no_means: A NO vote rolls the rate back to the voter-approval rate.
fiscal_impact: The ballot states a 4.88 percent increase but lists the added dollars as "$ -20.30," which does not match. We found no district explanation.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot opens with "This is a tax increase" (printed in capitals), as state law requires. The official wording also seems to contain an error: a 4.88% increase described as an additional negative $20.30. Otherwise it works like any tax rate election: FOR keeps the adopted rate, AGAINST rolls it back to the voter-approval rate.
